title: Simulation Task
description: Develop a multi-agent simulation system that models the spread of mask-wearing behavior through social networks.
simulation_focus: Predict agents' mask-wearing behavior over day 30 - day 39 (last ten days) based on their attributes, social connections, and past behavior
Model information propagation and behavioral changes triggered by social influence and government intervention starting on Day 10

data_files.agent_attributes.csv: Contains demographic and behavioral attributes of each agent, including age, occupation, risk perception, and social connection counts
data_files.social_network.json: Contains structured data representing a social network. Each entry corresponds to a user (identified by a unique integer ID), and the values describe the different types of relationships that user has with others. Data Structure: The top-level structure is a dictionary ({} in JSON). Keys: Each key is a unique user ID (as an integer, e.g., 0, 1, 2, etc.). Values: Each value is another dictionary with the following fields: "family": a list of user IDs representing family connections. "work_school": a list of user IDs representing colleagues or schoolmates. "community": a list of user IDs representing community-level acquaintances. "all": a merged list of all user IDs connected to the user across the three categories above.
data_files.train_data.csv: Time series data for the first 30 days, used for training the model

RMSE.description: Root Mean Square Error measuring overall predictive accuracy of mask adoption rates
RMSE.interpretation: Directly interpretable as percentage deviations due to the 0-1 range

Peak Adoption Rate Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting maximum mask adoption during intervention

Time-to-Peak Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting the time lag from intervention to peak behavior change

key_patterns.name: Multiplex network with heterogeneous degrees
key_patterns.description: Agents have separate degree counts for family, work/school, and community layers. Family degrees are typically smaller and denser; work/school moderate; community broader and more heterogeneous.
key_patterns.relevance: Layer-specific influence and contact frequency should be modeled; degrees guide per-layer interaction rates and influence weights.

key_patterns.name: Demographic and occupational structure
key_patterns.description: Age_group derives from age and, along with occupation, likely correlates with which layer dominates an agent’s connections (e.g., students: higher work/school ties).
key_patterns.relevance: Supports homophily-based network generation and layer participation; stratified dynamics may differ by age/occupation.

key_patterns.name: Risk perception heterogeneity
key_patterns.description: risk_perception varies in [0,1] and is expected to correlate positively with initial_mask_wearing.
key_patterns.relevance: Use as an individual susceptibility parameter for adoption thresholds or logistic coefficients.

key_patterns.name: Initial seeding of mask wearing
key_patterns.description: initial_mask_wearing provides day-0 seeds that may cluster via homophily when mapped onto the network.
key_patterns.relevance: Sets initial conditions for diffusion; clustering impacts early cascade dynamics.

key_patterns.name: Behavioral inertia
key_patterns.description: In the panel time series, wearing_mask tends to persist across days (high probability to remain wearing once adopted).
key_patterns.relevance: Model needs separate adoption and abandonment hazards; persistence affects equilibrium prevalence and diffusion speed.

key_patterns.name: Information exposure effect
key_patterns.description: received_info is associated with higher same-day or next-day adoption probability.
key_patterns.relevance: Parameterize an exogenous information shock effect that boosts adoption hazard independent of peer exposure.

key_patterns.name: Directedness and reciprocity in adjacency
key_patterns.description: Adjacency JSON may contain non-reciprocated ties; overlaps across layers can occur.
key_patterns.relevance: Decide whether to symmetrize edges for undirected influence or keep directionality; reciprocity influences exposure counts.

key_patterns.name: Heavy-tailed contact heterogeneity
key_patterns.description: Community connections likely exhibit over-dispersion (a few very connected agents).
key_patterns.relevance: Super-spreader-like influence on behavior diffusion; motivates negative binomial degree models and targeted interventions.

key_distributions.name: Per-layer degree distributions
key_distributions.description: Distributions of family_connections, work_school_connections, community_connections (and their sum).
key_distributions.parameters: For each layer: mean, variance, over-dispersion (fit Poisson vs Negative Binomial), and quantiles (p10, p50, p90).

key_distributions.name: Risk perception
key_distributions.description: Continuous propensity in [0,1]; appropriate to model with a Beta distribution.
key_distributions.parameters: Beta(a, b) estimated from risk_perception via method-of-moments or MLE; also store mean and std.

key_distributions.name: Age and occupation
key_distributions.description: Discrete distributions over age_group and occupation categories.
key_distributions.parameters: Category proportions; cross-tabulation P(occupation | age_group) for mixing.

key_distributions.name: Initial mask prevalence
key_distributions.description: Share of agents wearing a mask at day 0 (from time series) or initial_mask_wearing in attributes.
key_distributions.parameters: p0 = mean(wearing_mask at day 0); compare with mean(initial_mask_wearing) if both available.

key_distributions.name: Adoption and abandonment hazards
key_distributions.description: Daily transition probabilities estimated from panel data.
key_distributions.parameters: P(adopt | not wearing, received_info), P(adopt | not wearing, no info); P(abandon | wearing); optionally stratified by demographics.

key_distributions.name: Wearing spell lengths
key_distributions.description: Distribution of consecutive days wearing a mask after adoption.
key_distributions.parameters: Geometric or discrete Weibull parameters; median and tail behavior to capture persistence.

key_distributions.name: Information exposure frequency
key_distributions.description: Distribution of received_info across agents and days; may be bursty.
key_distributions.parameters: Per-day rate λ_info, fraction of agents ever exposed, and clustering (run-lengths of info days).

key_relationships.relationship: Higher risk_perception is associated with higher probability of adopting masks.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate logistic coefficient β_risk > 0; expected medium-to-strong.

key_relationships.relationship: Exposure to information increases adoption probability contemporaneously or with a 1-day lag.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate treatment effect β_info > 0; expected medium.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher fraction of masked neighbors raises adoption probability; layer effects differ (family strongest).
key_relationships.strength: Estimate peer influence coefficients β_family > β_work > β_comm; expected small-to-medium per neighbor, cumulative effect can be large.

key_relationships.relationship: Certain groups (e.g., students, young adults) concentrate ties in work/school, older groups in family/community.
key_relationships.strength: Compute correlations or regression of degrees on demographics; expected medium.
High; persistence probability substantially exceeds adoption probability.

key_relationships.relationship: Non-reciprocated ties imply asymmetric exposure unless symmetrized.
key_relationships.strength: Quantify reciprocity rate; if low, directed modeling is warranted.

use_provided_network.value: if adjacency JSON present then true else false
use_provided_network.notes: Prefer empirical adjacency when available; otherwise generate a synthetic multiplex network using agent_attributes degree targets.

edge_directionality.value: symmetrize_family; consider directed for work_school and community
edge_directionality.notes: Family ties likely mutual; for other layers decide based on measured reciprocity fraction. Symmetrizing simplifies peer averaging.

per_layer_degree_sequences.value: use empirical degrees from adjacency JSON or targets from agent_attributes
per_layer_degree_sequences.notes: If generating network, enforce even sum of degrees per layer (stub-matching) and correct infeasible degrees.

degree_distribution_models.value: Negative Binomial for community; Poisson/NegBin for work/school; small-variance for family
degree_distribution_models.notes: Fit by MLE; use for synthetic degree sampling and robustness analysis.

homophily_mixing.value: estimate mixing matrices by age_group and occupation per layer
homophily_mixing.notes: If adjacency not available, derive target assortativity from observed co-distributions of degrees and demographics.

layer_overlap_rate.value: fraction of dyads appearing in multiple layers
layer_overlap_rate.notes: If overlap is high, adjust influence to avoid double-counting across layers.

clustering_coefficient.value: estimate global and per-layer clustering; add triadic closure if needed
clustering_coefficient.notes: If generating networks, use clustering-enhanced configuration models to match observed clustering.

initial_mask_prevalence.notes: Use time-series as ground truth when available; reconcile discrepancies with attributes.

risk_perception_distribution.notes: Use method-of-moments or MLE; store (a,b) for sampling individual thresholds.

adoption_model_form.value: logistic: P(mask_t=1) = σ(α + ρ·mask_{t-1} + β_info·info_t + Σ_l β_l·frac_masked_neighbors_l + γ'X_i)
adoption_model_form.notes: ρ captures persistence; X_i can include risk_perception and demographics; when peer fractions not observed, estimate α, ρ, β_info first and calibrate β_l via simulation.

persistence_parameter.value: ρ estimated from logistic transition model
persistence_parameter.notes: Expect ρ > 0 and sizable; governs stickiness once adopted.

abandonment_probability.value: P(mask_t=0 | mask_{t-1}=1) estimated as 1 - P(continue wearing)
abandonment_probability.notes: Estimate overall and stratified by demographics for heterogeneity.

peer_influence_weights.source: calibrated using simulated method of moments against time-series prevalence curves
peer_influence_weights.notes: Initialize prior weights e.g., family>work>community (e.g., 0.5,0.3,0.2) then refine to match observed adoption dynamics.

information_effect.value: β_info (log-odds) from logistic model with received_info
information_effect.notes: Consider both contemporaneous and 1-day lag terms; choose based on AIC/BIC.

individual_susceptibility_mapping.value: θ_i = f(risk_perception_i) with f decreasing threshold or positive logit coefficient on risk_perception
individual_susceptibility_mapping.notes: Option 1: threshold models where adoption if weighted neighbor fraction > θ_i = 1 - risk_perception_i; Option 2: logistic coefficient β_risk.

daily_contacts_per_layer.value: c_l(i) = min(cmax_l, k_l(i) * s_l) where k_l is degree in layer l
daily_contacts_per_layer.notes: Choose scale s_l to reflect frequency (family highest). Calibrate s_l to match plausible daily contact counts if available.

layer_influence_weights.source: theory-driven prior; refined via calibration to match adoption trajectory
layer_influence_weights.notes: Re-weight during calibration; ensure sum to 1 after adjusting for edge overlap.

update_scheme.value: synchronous daily updates with exposure computed from previous day
update_scheme.notes: Avoids simultaneity bias; can also test asynchronous stochastic updates in sensitivity analysis.

info_arrival_rate.notes: Use as baseline Poisson/Bernoulli rate for exogenous info events; allow targeted rates by occupation.

campaign_targeting.value: optional: elevate info rates for selected demographics/occupations
campaign_targeting.source: policy scenario design; informed by occupation distribution
campaign_targeting.notes: Use to test intervention strategies; not identifiable from data without additional context.

measurement_error_mask_state.value: assume zero or small false positive/negative rates; sensitivity analysis only
measurement_error_mask_state.notes: If external validation exists, incorporate; otherwise keep at 0 and vary in robustness checks.

missing_data_handling.value: forward-fill within spells; drop isolated missing days; verify one row per (agent,day)
missing_data_handling.notes: Ensure consistent transition estimation; document imputation rate.

preprocessing_steps.purpose: Ensure total_connections equals sum of layer degrees; check ranges (risk_perception in [0,1]); parse booleans; handle missing values.

If adjacency JSON exists, load and compute per-layer degrees, reciprocity, overlap, clustering. If not, generate per-layer graphs via configuration models using degree targets and homophily constraints.
Join time-series and attributes by agent_id; drop agents without overlap or create placeholders.
Verify one row per (agent, day); handle missing days; compute spells, daily transitions, and lagged variables (mask_{t-1}, received_info_{t}, received_info_{t-1}).

preprocessing_steps.step: Compute peer exposure series (if network provided)
preprocessing_steps.purpose: For each agent-day, compute fraction of masked neighbors per layer from previous day to use in regression/calibration.
Create categorical dummies for age_group and occupation; compute degrees per layer for use as controls.

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Use a two-stage strategy. Stage 1: Estimate individual-level transition dynamics without peer terms using the panel: logistic regression or mixed effects model of wearing_mask_t on wearing_mask_{t-1}, received_info_t (and lag), risk_perception, demographics, and optionally agent random intercepts. Extract baseline intercept, persistence (ρ), information effect (β_info), and risk coefficient (β_risk). Stage 2: Calibrate peer influence and layer weights using simulation-based methods. If adjacency is available, augment the regression with lagged peer exposure fractions per layer to estimate β_family, β_work, β_community directly. If not available, perform simulated method of moments or approximate Bayesian computation: generate networks consistent with degree distributions and homophily; simulate adoption with candidate β_l and layer weights; minimize distance between observed and simulated moments (time path of prevalence, adoption and abandonment hazards, spell-length distribution, and cross-sectional variance by occupation/age). Iterate until convergence. Fit degree distribution models (Poisson/NegBin) and Beta distribution for risk_perception for input sampling. Use cross-validation on days to guard against overfitting.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Hold out a block of days (e.g., last 20%) and/or a subset of agents for out-of-sample validation. Compare simulated vs observed: (1) aggregate prevalence over time, (2) daily adoption and abandonment rates, (3) distribution of wearing spell lengths, (4) stratified prevalence by age_group and occupation, (5) if network available, spatial clustering of behavior (e.g., Moran’s I or assortativity of mask state). Perform posterior predictive checks and sensitivity analysis on layer weights and network symmetrization. Report calibration error metrics (RMSE of prevalence curve, KL divergence of spell-length distribution).
key_variables_to_calibrate: risk_perception mapping (β_risk or threshold function parameters)
homophily mixing strengths and network symmetrization choice

file_summaries:
Semantic metadata summary for agent_attributes.csv

- Overall data structure and type
  - Flat CSV; one row per agent (unique agent_id).
  - Columns include integers, floats, booleans, and categorical strings.
  - No explicit network edges; only per-layer degree counts.

- Meaning of keys/columns
  - agent_id (int): Unique identifier for each agent.
  - age (int): Agent’s age in years.
  - age_group (string): Categorical bin of age (e.g., Youth, Young Adult, Middle Age); redundant with age.
  - occupation (string): Socioeconomic/role category (e.g., Student, Blue Collar, White Collar); useful for homophily and layer assignment.
  - risk_perception (float 0–1): Propensity to adopt mask-wearing given perceived risk; higher implies easier adoption.
  - initial_mask_wearing (bool): Initial behavioral state at t0.
  - family_connections (int): Target degree in the family/household layer.
  - work_school_connections (int): Target degree in the work/school layer.
  - community_connections (int): Target degree in the community/social layer.
  - total_connections (int): Redundant; equals family + work_school + community.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - Multi-layer network semantics: the three connection columns indicate degrees per layer; total_connections is the sum across layers.
  - age_group is derived from age; may guide layer participation (e.g., students with higher school ties).
  - No nested records; relationships are implied, not enumerated.

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agent construction: instantiate agents with attributes (id, age/age_group, occupation, risk_perception, initial_mask_wearing).
  - Network generation: build a three-layer graph using the per-layer degree targets (e.g., configuration model per layer with homophily by age/occupation). Ensure degree feasibility and reciprocity; total_connections is a validation check.
  - Interaction dynamics:
    - Influence weights by layer (e.g., family > work/school > community) and contact frequency derived from layer degrees.
    - Adoption rule: probability/threshold for switching to mask-wearing as a function of risk_perception, fraction of masked neighbors per layer, and layer weights. initial_mask_wearing seeds the diffusion.
    - Heterogeneity by demographics/occupation can modulate susceptibility, influence, or contact rates.
  - Validation/consistency: verify total_connections equals the sum of layer degrees; handle agents with zero degree in specific layers; note that age_group/occupation may contain edge cases and should not be assumed to be strictly realistic.

- Overall data structure and type:
  - JSON object representing a social network as adjacency lists.
  - Top-level keys are agent identifiers (as strings), each mapping to an object of contact lists.
- Meaning of keys or columns:
  - family: list of agent IDs with familial ties to the focal agent.
  - work_school: list of agent IDs representing workplace/school contacts.
  - community: list of agent IDs for broader community ties (neighbors, social groups, etc.).
  - all: deduplicated union of family, work_school, and community contacts for that agent.
- Relationships or nested elements:
  - Each agent node contains three layer-specific neighbor lists plus a flattened “all” list.
  - Values are integer agent IDs; no explicit edge weights or directions are provided.
  - Reciprocity is not guaranteed by the data (an agent may list another who does not list them back); treat as directed unless you explicitly symmetrize.
  - Potential overlap across layers is possible; “all” consolidates them.
- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions:
  - Define one agent per top-level key (ID space appears to be roughly 0–999).
  - Build a multiplex network with three layers (family, work/school, community); use “all” for fast neighbor iteration but retain layer labels for dynamics.
  - Assign layer-specific influence/contact parameters (e.g., family: strongest/highest frequency, work_school: medium, community: weakest/lowest frequency).
  - Schedule interactions by sampling neighbors per layer each timestep; compute mask adoption updates based on neighbors’ mask status with layer-weighted influence.
  - If modeling undirected influence, consider symmetrizing edges; otherwise, keep as directed for asymmetric exposure.
  - No agent attributes are included; initialize mask-wearing states, susceptibility, and compliance parameters externally.

- Overall data structure and type
  - CSV file in long/record format; each row is a time-stamped observation for one agent.
  - Granularity: one row per (agent_id, day). Primary key should be the tuple (agent_id, day).
  - Data types: day (int, discrete timestep), agent_id (int), wearing_mask (boolean), received_info (boolean).

- Meaning of keys or columns
  - day: Discrete simulation timestep (e.g., t = 0, 1, 2, …).
  - agent_id: Unique identifier for an agent (node) in the social network.
  - wearing_mask: Agent’s behavioral state at that day (1 = wearing a mask, 0 = not wearing).
  - received_info: Whether the agent was exposed to an information event that day (e.g., message/campaign/peer message); likely a per-day flag, not cumulative.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - Flat (no nested structures). Time series relationships are implied by grouping rows by agent_id and ordering by day.
  - No explicit network structure or neighbor relations in this file; social ties must come from another source or be synthetically generated.
  - Implicit temporal dependency: wearing_mask(t) depends on past states and possibly on received_info(t); may also depend on peers (not represented here).

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agent initialization: Use day 0 records to set initial mask-wearing state per agent.
  - Transition modeling: Estimate adoption and abandonment probabilities P(mask_t | mask_{t-1}, received_info_t, agent) from the panel data (e.g., Markov/logistic models). Consider agent-level heterogeneity if enough history per agent exists.
  - Information effects: Quantify the causal/associative impact of received_info on same-day or next-day adoption, informing rules for exogenous information shocks or campaign scheduling.
  - Persistence/inertia: Infer duration dependence (e.g., probability to continue wearing once adopted) from consecutive days.
  - Missing components: Since network edges and peer exposure are not included, the simulation should:
    - Ingest or generate a network (adjacency) separately.
    - Define peer influence rules using the simulated neighbor mask rates, combining them with the calibrated individual and information-driven transition probabilities.
  - Data hygiene assumptions: Ensure one unique row per (agent_id, day); handle boolean parsing (true/false); check for missing days per agent and decide on imputation or skipping in model fitting.
